hottake: Pineapple on pizza is not the real problem — the real problem is people who hate it.
Breakfast food tastes better at dinner than at actual breakfast.
Adding cheese to almost anything makes it better.
Spicy food is not really about taste — it is about proving something.
Ordering the same thing every time at a restaurant is a sign of self-awareness, not boring taste.
Sharing food off someone else's plate without asking is completely unacceptable.
Instant noodles deserve way more respect than they get.
If the food is good enough, the atmosphere of a restaurant does not matter at all.
The person who finishes their meal first should have to sit in silence while others catch up.
Drinks are always better with ice, even in winter.
Dessert should come before the main course — life is short.
People who say they 'don't have a favourite food' are lying.
Ghosting someone you barely know is perfectly acceptable.
Long-distance relationships almost never truly work out.
You can fall genuinely in love with someone you have never met in person.
People who arrive exactly on time are more annoying than people who are five minutes late.
Crying in front of others is a sign of strength, not weakness.
Complimenting a stranger is almost always welcome, not awkward.
The best friendships need no explanation after a long silence.
Being liked by everyone is a red flag.
You cannot truly know someone until you have travelled with them.
Most people are far lonelier than they are willing to admit.
A person's true character is revealed by how they treat waiters and cashiers.
The phrase 'We should catch up sometime' almost never actually means it.
Being early to everything is a form of social anxiety, not politeness.
A person who has never been heartbroken has never truly been in love.
TikTok has done more damage to attention spans than any drug ever did.
Replying with just 'K' to a message is passive-aggressive, no matter the context.
Reacting to someone's message with 👍 is the digital equivalent of a dismissive nod.
Voice notes should require the other person's permission before you send one.
Checking your phone first thing every morning is one of the worst habits a person can have.
Social media makes people more lonely, not less.
Everyone performs a different version of themselves online — and that is perfectly fine.
Deleting all social media for a month would make most people genuinely happier.
Online arguments almost never actually change anyone's mind.
A person's texting style tells you more about them than their CV.
The most productive people are rarely the busiest ones.
Homework should be banned for everyone under 14.
A university degree is no longer worth the time or money for most careers.
Most job interviews tell you almost nothing useful about how someone will actually perform.
You should always try to negotiate your salary — no exceptions.
Passion for your work is overrated. Decent pay and good hours matter far more.
Open-plan offices are one of the worst ideas in modern workplace history.
Arriving 10 minutes early to a meeting you did not call is just unpaid work.
The best meetings are the ones that could have been a short email.
Four-day work weeks would make most people more productive, not less.
People who say 'I don't care what others think' usually care the most.
Being bored is actually essential for creativity.
Success in life is mostly about luck, not skill or hard work.
Most adults are not nearly as grown-up as they pretend to be.
Having two or three real friends is far better than having twenty casual ones.
It is more important to be interesting than to be nice.
People change over time, but not nearly as much as they like to claim.
Regret teaches you more than success ever does.
Everyone secretly has at least one truly terrible opinion they will never admit to.
Saying sorry too often actually makes people trust you less, not more.
Small talk is not a waste of time — it is how trust gets built.
The funniest people in the room are almost always hiding something painful.
People who walk slowly in the middle of a crowded pavement are the real villains of society.
Movie sequels are almost always worse than the original — no exceptions.
Spoilers actually make a story more enjoyable to experience, not less.
The best music was almost certainly made before you were born.
Horror films are far more effective watched alone than with a group of friends.
Celebrities do not owe their fans any explanation about their private lives.
Reboots and remakes are completely lazy — and yet we watch every single one.
Silence in a good conversation is not awkward — it means both people are comfortable.
Cats are smarter than dogs. Dogs are just more emotionally needy.
Bad weather makes people more creative and productive, not less.
The last piece of shared food should always go to whoever ate the least.

sophies.situation: Your best friend has been cheating on their partner for six months. Their partner — who is also your friend — just told you they are planning to propose next week.
sophies.a: Stay silent. Your loyalty belongs to your best friend, and it is not your relationship.
sophies.b: Tell the partner the truth before the proposal happens. They deserve to know.

sophies.situation: Your father has just been diagnosed with a serious illness and needs daily care. The promotion you have worked eight years for was just announced — and it requires you to move abroad immediately.
sophies.a: Accept the promotion. Your father has other family who can help.
sophies.b: Turn it down and go home to care for your father. The career can wait.

sophies.situation: You discover your company has been knowingly selling a product that is dangerous to children. Your boss tells you that if you speak to anyone about it, you will be fired and blacklisted from the industry.
sophies.a: Stay quiet. You have a family to support and no other job lined up.
sophies.b: Report it to the authorities, even if it means losing everything you have built.

sophies.situation: You have been with your partner for five years and love them deeply. You just found a message on their phone showing they kissed someone else at a work event last month. They have been acting completely normal ever since.
sophies.a: Confront them directly. You need the truth, even if it destroys the relationship.
sophies.b: Say nothing. One mistake should not erase five years of love.

sophies.situation: Your younger sibling confesses that they caused a hit-and-run accident years ago that seriously injured someone. The victim spent a year in hospital and still walks with a limp. Your sibling has completely changed their life since then.
sophies.a: Encourage them to go to the police and confess. The victim deserves justice.
sophies.b: Keep their secret. What good does it do now to destroy your sibling's life?

sophies.situation: Your closest friend has been in a relationship that has slowly become controlling and isolating. They refuse to see it as a problem. Their partner has never been violent — yet — but you are genuinely afraid of what may come.
sophies.a: Contact their family and explain your fears, even if it costs you the friendship.
sophies.b: Respect their wishes and stay available without pushing. It is their life.

sophies.situation: You are the best man at a wedding. The night before the ceremony, the groom privately tells you he is not sure he still loves the bride — but everything is paid for, and both families have flown in from across the world.
sophies.a: Tell him to call it off. A marriage built on doubt will only cause more pain.
sophies.b: Tell him cold feet are normal and push him to go through with it.

sophies.situation: Your elderly parent has just been diagnosed with terminal cancer and has about six months to live. They have no idea and are happily making plans for the future. The doctor asks you to decide whether they should be told.
sophies.a: Tell them the truth. They deserve to know and to say their goodbyes properly.
sophies.b: Let them stay happy and unaware for whatever time they have left.

sophies.situation: Your closest colleague confides that they have been secretly using drugs and it is affecting their work. They operate heavy machinery. Last week there was a near-accident that nobody else noticed. They beg you not to tell anyone.
sophies.a: Keep their secret and try to support them privately. Reporting will destroy their life.
sophies.b: Report it to management. Everyone's safety matters more than one person's secret.

sophies.situation: Your partner of three years says they will end the relationship if you take a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity — a year abroad that you have been dreaming about since childhood.
sophies.a: Give up the trip. This relationship is more important than any dream.
sophies.b: Go anyway. If the relationship cannot survive one year apart, it was never strong enough.

sophies.situation: You are on a jury. The evidence clearly proves the defendant is guilty. But you learn they committed the crime to feed their starving children after every other option had failed. A guilty verdict means a long prison sentence.
sophies.a: Vote guilty. The law must be applied equally to everyone, no matter the circumstances.
sophies.b: Vote not guilty. No law should imprison a parent for feeding their children.

sophies.situation: A colleague you barely know has been falsely accused of something serious at work. You know the truth — but speaking up means admitting you were somewhere you were not supposed to be that day.
sophies.a: Come forward with the truth, even if it exposes where you really were.
sophies.b: Stay silent. You do not know this person well enough to risk your own reputation.

sophies.situation: You find your teenager's private diary left open on the table. You have been deeply worried about them for weeks — they have been withdrawn, sad, and distant.
sophies.a: Read it. You are their parent and their safety is more important than their privacy.
sophies.b: Put it back unopened. Trust is the foundation of your relationship with your child.

sophies.situation: Your best friend has spent three years writing a novel and asks for your honest opinion before sending it to publishers. In your view, the book is genuinely terrible and will certainly be rejected everywhere. They are clearly very proud of it.
sophies.a: Tell them the full truth now. Rejection letters from strangers will be far more painful.
sophies.b: Tell them it is wonderful and encourage them to try. Dreams are worth protecting.

sophies.situation: You are walking alone late at night and see a man aggressively threatening a woman on an empty street. You have no phone signal and no weapon.
sophies.a: Step in immediately. You cannot walk past and do nothing.
sophies.b: Keep moving as fast as you can to find help. Getting yourself hurt helps nobody.

sophies.situation: Your parent asks directly whether you like their new partner. You believe the new partner is manipulative and possibly dangerous. Your parent seems genuinely happy for the first time in years.
sophies.a: Tell them the full truth, even if it creates distance between you.
sophies.b: Say you are happy for them. You might be wrong, and they deserve to feel joy.

sophies.situation: You discover on the morning of your wedding that your future spouse once committed a serious crime for which they were never caught. They were very young. They deeply regret it. The victim is someone you know.
sophies.a: Go ahead with the wedding. People can change, and you love who they are today.
sophies.b: Call it off. You cannot build a marriage on a secret of this size.

sophies.situation: Your brother calls from abroad in tears. He has done something illegal — nothing violent, but serious — and asks you to lie to the police if they contact you. He says the truth will send him to prison.
sophies.a: Lie for him. He is your brother and you will not be the one who sends him to prison.
sophies.b: Tell the truth. You will not commit a crime for anyone, even family.

sophies.situation: Your friend has been trying to have a baby through IVF for three years, with no success. They are about to spend their entire life savings on one final attempt. You genuinely believe it will not work.
sophies.a: Tell them exactly what you think, even if it destroys their last hope.
sophies.b: Say nothing. This is their decision and their hope to hold onto.

sophies.situation: Your ageing parent has started showing signs of memory loss and got lost on a familiar road last week. They become furious whenever driving is mentioned. Nothing has been officially diagnosed and their licence is still valid.
sophies.a: Report your concerns to their doctor and ask that the licence be reviewed.
sophies.b: Say nothing. Taking away their independence will break them. They deserve dignity.

sophies.situation: You are a journalist and have just found proof of a story that will make your career — but publishing it will destroy the reputation of an innocent person who happens to be connected to the real story.
sophies.a: Publish it. The public has a right to know and this is your job.
sophies.b: Bury the story. Some careers are not worth what they cost other people.

sophies.situation: You and your partner have been trying to have a child for years. You discover that the reason you cannot conceive is your partner's health. They do not know yet. Telling them will change everything.
sophies.a: Tell them immediately. They have an absolute right to know the truth about their own body.
sophies.b: Keep the information to yourself for now. You need time to figure out how to handle it.

sophies.situation: The mentor who gave you your first job — and changed your life — asks you to be a reference for a senior role. You have heard from a reliable source that they behaved very badly toward a former colleague. You were not there and cannot be certain.
sophies.a: Refuse to be a reference and explain your reason honestly.
sophies.b: Give the glowing reference. You owe this person everything, and you are not certain of the story.

sophies.situation: Your closest friend is going for the same promotion as you. You discover by accident that they lied on their application in a way that will almost certainly get them the position over you. Only you know.
sophies.a: Report the lie to HR. The position should go to whoever truly deserves it.
sophies.b: Stay silent. You will not betray a close friendship for your own career gain.

sophies.situation: You are in a job interview your family desperately needs you to get. The interviewer makes a discriminatory comment about a group you belong to — but cannot tell by looking at you. Speaking up will almost certainly end the interview.
sophies.a: Speak up immediately. You will not sit through discrimination for any salary.
sophies.b: Stay silent, get the job, and fight bigger battles from a position of strength.

sophies.situation: Your teenage child comes home shaken and admits they watched a classmate get seriously bullied and did nothing. The victim was badly hurt. The school is now investigating and asking all students what they saw.
sophies.a: Tell your child to go to the school and tell the full truth immediately.
sophies.b: Tell your child to say nothing. Protecting your own child comes before everything else.

sophies.situation: You are deeply in debt and about to lose your home. A stranger drops a bag and disappears into a crowd. Inside you find $20,000 in cash — clearly not legally obtained — with no way to identify the owner.
sophies.a: Keep it. You need it more than whoever lost it, and they were clearly no saint.
sophies.b: Hand it in to the police. Money like this never comes without consequences.

sophies.situation: You have lived in your adopted country for twenty years and built your entire life here. You discover that due to an old paperwork error, your citizenship is technically not valid. Nobody is looking for you.
sophies.a: Come forward immediately and try to correct it legally, whatever the cost.
sophies.b: Stay silent. You have earned your place here and nobody is coming for you.

sophies.situation: Your best friend is about to make a business investment that you are almost certain will fail and leave them bankrupt. They have not asked for your opinion and seem completely committed to the plan.
sophies.a: Tell them exactly what you think, even if they resent you for it.
sophies.b: Say nothing. They are an adult and it is not your place to interfere.

sophies.situation: You find proof that a very close family member has been lying to the entire family for years about something significant — money, identity, or the past. Revealing it will shatter everything. Staying silent means living with the lie.
sophies.a: Bring it into the open. The family deserves to know the truth, however painful.
sophies.b: Keep it to yourself. Some truths do more damage than the lies they replace.

sophies.situation: Your sibling has been in a serious accident and is brain-dead. The doctors say there is no chance of recovery. They could save five other lives if you agree to organ donation. Your parents are unreachable abroad and the doctors need an answer within the hour.
sophies.a: Give consent for the donation. Five lives matter more than keeping your sibling on a machine.
sophies.b: Wait for your parents, however long it takes. This decision is not yours alone to make.

sophies.situation: You work for a pharmaceutical company and discover that data in a major drug trial has been secretly altered to hide serious side effects. The drug is about to be approved and millions of people will use it. Speaking out will likely end your career and expose you to legal action.
sophies.a: Go public with the evidence. Millions of patients matter more than your career.
sophies.b: Resign quietly and say nothing. You cannot fight this system alone and you will lose.

sophies.situation: Your partner has been in a coma for nine months with no brain activity. The doctors say recovery is impossible. They are kept alive by machines. Your partner left no living will. Their parents want to keep the machines on indefinitely. You must make a final decision.
sophies.a: Make the decision to switch off the machines and let them go in peace.
sophies.b: Respect the parents' wishes. You will not be the one who ends their child's life.

sophies.situation: You are on an overloaded lifeboat after a disaster. There is room for exactly one more person. In the water you can see two people — a young mother holding a baby, and your own elderly parent. The boat cannot hold both.
sophies.a: Pull in the young mother and her baby. There is no other choice you can live with.
sophies.b: Pull in your parent. You cannot abandon the person who raised you.

sophies.situation: Your best friend confides that they have been having thoughts of harming themselves. They are not in immediate danger but the situation is serious. They beg you not to tell anyone — and say that if you break their trust they will never speak to you again.
sophies.a: Break their trust and contact their family or a professional immediately. Their life matters more.
sophies.b: Respect their wishes, stay as close as possible, and support them yourself.

sophies.situation: You discover that the factory your entire town depends on for employment is secretly dumping toxic waste into the local river. Children downstream are getting sick. Reporting it will almost certainly shut the factory down and end the livelihoods of nearly everyone you know.
sophies.a: Report it to the authorities. The health of children comes before anyone's job.
sophies.b: Go to the factory owner privately first and demand they stop before you take any further action.

sophies.situation: Your parent has just died and you discover they secretly had a second family in another city for over twenty years. The other family does not know your parent has passed away. Their children are your half-siblings. They have a right to grieve — but the truth will shatter everything.
sophies.a: Contact the other family. They deserve to know the truth and to say goodbye.
sophies.b: Let them live without ever knowing. What they do not know cannot hurt them now.

sophies.situation: You are reviewing applications for a life-changing scholarship. The top application is clearly the best — but several paragraphs are copied from an obscure old source that the rest of the committee would never find. The second-place applicant is also talented and genuinely deserving.
sophies.a: Disqualify the top application. Plagiarism is plagiarism, regardless of the circumstances.
sophies.b: Award it anyway. The copied lines were minor and the application is still far and away the best.

sophies.situation: You find out you carry a genetic condition that your future children have a 50% chance of inheriting. It is serious but manageable. Your partner desperately wants children and has never asked about your family medical history. You have not told them.
sophies.a: Tell them immediately, even if it changes your entire future together.
sophies.b: Say nothing for now. Many people live full lives with this condition and it is your private health information.

sophies.situation: Your teenage child has been accepted into a prestigious sports academy that could lead to a professional career. But the training means leaving school, losing normal friendships, and enormous pressure from age 14. Your child is certain they want to go. You are not.
sophies.a: Support their dream fully. It is their life and you will back them completely.
sophies.b: Make them wait until 18 to choose. They are too young to give up a normal childhood.

sophies.situation: During a private conversation, your phone accidentally recorded your manager making comments that prove years of discrimination against a colleague who is about to be unfairly dismissed. You had no right to record the conversation. Using the recording could save your colleague's career.
sophies.a: Share the recording with HR. How you obtained it does not change what it proves.
sophies.b: Delete it. You had no right to that recording and using it will only turn everything against you.

sophies.situation: A stranger sits next to you on a long flight and, believing they will never see you again, confesses to something terrible they did years ago — something that caused great harm to a person you happen to know personally. The stranger does not know this connection.
sophies.a: Tell them exactly who you are and what their actions did to someone you love.
sophies.b: Say nothing. They will carry the weight of their own conscience without your help.

sophies.situation: Your child has been accepted into their dream university on a financial-need scholarship. You have just received an inheritance that technically disqualifies them — but nobody asked and you did not volunteer the information. The scholarship covers everything.
sophies.a: Contact the university and declare the inheritance. Your child must earn their place honestly.
sophies.b: Say nothing. The scholarship system is deeply imperfect and your child genuinely deserves this.

sophies.situation: A close friend who is a teacher has been having an inappropriate relationship with a 17-year-old student. The student appears willing. Your friend is about to get married and their partner is pregnant. You are the only one who knows.
sophies.a: Report it to the school and authorities without delay.
sophies.b: Confront your friend directly and give them the chance to end it before you act.

sophies.situation: You discover your 16-year-old child has been secretly sending money every month to a person they met online — someone you have never heard of, in another country. Your child refuses to discuss it and says you would not understand.
sophies.a: Cut off their access to money and report it to the police as a potential scam or worse.
sophies.b: Give them the chance to explain first. Cutting them off without listening will destroy their trust in you.

sophies.situation: You are a doctor in a crisis with one treatment left and two patients who critically need it tonight. One is a 78-year-old grandmother surrounded by family. The other is a 10-year-old child. Both will die without treatment. The decision falls entirely to you.
sophies.a: Give the treatment to the child. They have their whole life ahead of them.
sophies.b: Give it to the grandmother. She arrived first and every human life deserves equal value.

sophies.situation: You are on a hiking trip and your friend twists their ankle badly in a remote area. It will be dark in two hours. You can carry them slowly toward the road, or leave them sheltered and run for help alone — but the weather is changing fast and you are not sure which choice is safer.
sophies.a: Leave them in a safe spot and run for help. You can move faster alone and get back sooner.
sophies.b: Stay together no matter what. You will not leave your friend alone in the dark.

sophies.situation: Your friend has spent years convinced that their ex ended the relationship unfairly and treated them badly. You know the real story — your friend was controlling and unkind in ways they have never acknowledged. They are now in a new relationship and the same patterns are emerging.
sophies.a: Tell them the truth about why their last relationship really ended, even if it destroys your friendship.
sophies.b: Say nothing. People have to discover their own patterns in their own time.

sophies.situation: You discover that your own parent — who you have always deeply respected — reported a neighbour to the authorities decades ago for political reasons, knowing the accusation was false. The neighbour lost everything. That neighbour's family still lives nearby.
sophies.a: Confront your parent and push them to make some form of amends, however late.
sophies.b: Let it stay in the past. Your parent is old. Nothing you do now will undo what happened.

sophies.situation: You find out your closest friend has been secretly in contact with your ex-partner — the one who hurt you deeply — for over a year. They say they were trying to protect you by keeping it quiet. You are not sure whether to believe them.
sophies.a: End the friendship. The secret alone is a betrayal, regardless of the reason.
sophies.b: Hear them out fully before deciding anything. People keep secrets for complicated reasons.
